items.title: Legislative risk continues to cloud BTR’s capital outlook; here's why
items.description: Despite securing carve-outs from the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act 's institutional investor ban, build-to-rent (BTR) and single-family rental (SFR) operators continue to grapple with lingering legislative uncertainty that weighs on capital availability and new construction, both of which dramatically lag 2025 levels. According to the National Apartment Association ’s Q3 2026 Market Pulse , released Nov. 5, BTR units under construction fell 18.5% year over year, newly completed units declined 40.2% and sales volume of communities dropped 51.5%. Even against a broader nationwide slowdown in residential construction , the declining BTR pipeline continues to stand out. The industry's legislative uncertainty initially stemmed from an earlier version of ROAD, first introduced in March, that would have required investors and developers to sell newly built rental homes to individual buyers after seven years. The provision, among others, threatened the viability of the BTR business model, prompting investors to pull back from committing capital to new projects. Although the final version of ROAD exempted and protected BTR, uncertainty remains around how Treasury will implement the institutional investor ban, along with the potential for new federal and state legislation that could impose further institutional ownership restrictions. That lingering uncertainty continues to weigh on capital flowing into the industry. “I would say it hasn't normalized. In other words, it wasn't where it was a year ago, where capital was really flowing into the business,” Richard Ross, CEO at QuinnResidences , said when discussing the BTR market, in an interview with HousingWire TBD . “I almost don’t care what the rules are, as long as you tell me what the rules are,” Ross added. “With uncertainty, people just aren’t going to invest.” Uncertainty is still taking a toll Ross cited the Strait of Hormuz as a timely and illustrative comparison. While oil is still moving through the Strait, traffic remains more restricted than it was a year ago. BTR, he suggested, finds itself in a comparable position. “Capital's coming in, but it's not like it was pre-ROAD. The hope was that the regulatory process would give some clarity. And I think once it gets done, it will provide clarity, but you might remember this was only part one of the regulatory process,” he said, pointing to the prospects of a “ROAD 2.0” housing bill. “Until capital knows what the rules are, it's really hard for them to write checks. According to Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group , a builder, buyer and manager of single-family rentals, the capital environment for BTR had been flashing signs of softening even before the federal government introduced the idea of an institutional investor ban. New projects often came with modest returns, and rent growth was moderating or even falling across many high-growth Sun Belt markets. Add a steady drumbeat of policy risk from Washington, and many investors have simply taken their money elsewhere. “When you add policy uncertainty to the asset, it just doesn't have the return to pay for that,” Dobson said in an interview. Invitation Homes CEO Dallas Tanner also acknowledged that the capital environment hasn’t bounced back from an uncertain 2026 during the company’s Q3 2026 earnings call on October 29. "Capital's just starting to poke its eyes up after the ROAD Act piece of it. The market's still trying to find itself,” Tanner said. In a Q3 2026 Form 10-Q document filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on November 5, 2026, AMH also called out ongoing legislative uncertainty as a concern. “Further, the ROAD Act and the prospect of other such laws or regulations have adversely impacted and may in the future continue to adversely impact our access to capital markets and the attractiveness of our securities to certain investors,” the document warned. The uncertainty surrounding Treasury’s proposed rulemaking The U.S. Department of the Treasury , which implements the institutional investor ban included in ROAD, released a notice of proposed rulemaking in October that would grant BTR communities a range of notable exemptions from the ban. However, concerns remain about some of Treasury’s proposed interpretations. “If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, 'all right, built-to-rent is carved out.' But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Dobson said. Quinn Residences, in an open letter to Treasury, outlined several concerns about Treasury’s proposed rulemaking. Chief among them is a proposal to exempt purpose-built BTR communities from the institutional investor ban provided they haven’t been owner-occupied and are purchased within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy. Ross argued that this timeline isn’t sufficient, as the 18-month certificate-of-occupancy requirement could prevent institutional investors from acquiring purpose-built rental homes that have been operating as rentals for more than 18 months, even if they have never been owner-occupied. And building and stabilizing a community typically takes about 30 months, longer than the rule allows, Ross argued. The rule, therefore, could prevent subsequent sales of newly built BTR homes among institutional investors, effectively limiting the pool of potential buyers and potentially discouraging investment into new projects. Ross also signaled his opposition to another one of Treasury’s proposed rulemakings that would fail to exempt single-plat BTR communities zoned for multifamily use, despite congressional record statements indicating lawmakers intended those properties to be excluded from the ban. The increase reflected the removal of the RTP/I-40 Corridor’s 201,056-square-foot (sf) Charles Sanders Center, previously subleased to the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, from the life sciences inventory following its lease to BASIS Independent Schools, removing it from the life sciences inventory. Vacancy remained 160 bps below its Q3 2025 peak of 28.0%, supported by occupancy gains in recently delivered buildings and declining sublease vacancy. Overall net absorption remained positive for the fourth consecutive quarter, bringing year-to-date (YTD) occupancy gains to more than 233,000 sf as tenant move-outs remained limited. Prior quarter leasing translated into Q3 move-ins, including Google Fiber occupying nearly 25,000 sf at Eastridge – Building 300 and Jazz Pharmaceuticals occupying more than 18,800 sf at TBC – Building 4020. Strong new leasing will continue to support occupancy gains, especially as large manufacturing users complete build outs of their spaces. DG Matrix signed the quarter’s largest lease, taking nearly 55,000 sf at Southport 3 while diagnostics company Labcorp renewed for 33,500 sf at Eastridge – Building 100, contributing to nearly 64,000 sf of quarterly renewal activity. items.title: Hedge fund pressures Invitation Homes to speed up home sales
items.description: Activist investor Land & Buildings Investment Management is pressing single-family rental giant Invitation Homes to accelerate home sales, sharply increase capital returns and scale back growth plans, arguing the company’s stock trades at a steep discount to the value of its houses. In an open letter to shareholders released Monday, the Stamford, Connecticut-based hedge fund said it believes Invitation Homes is “among the most undervalued companies in the REIT sector” and criticized the board and management for what it called “complacency” and “half measures” in addressing the gap. Land & Buildings, which owns an undisclosed stake in Invitation Homes, is led by Jonathan Litt, a longtime activist in the real estate investment trust sector. Invitation Homes (NYSE: INVH) is the nation’s largest owner of single-family rental homes, with more than 80,000 properties concentrated in Sun Belt and other high-growth markets. Discount to home values at center of dispute Land & Buildings said the public market values Invitation Homes’ properties at roughly $270,000 per home, compared with an average sale price of about $460,000 on homes the company has sold since December 2025. That implies a discount of about 40%, according to the letter, which was disseminated via GlobeNewswire. The firm said it separately valued more than 90% of the company’s wholly owned portfolio, “address by address,” and arrived at an estimated average value of approximately $425,000 per home. That analysis underpins its net asset value estimate of about $45 per share, which Land & Buildings said is more than 65% above Invitation Homes’ current trading price even after assuming 6% selling costs on every home. “REITs with sound fundamentals and no distressed assets do not trade at such a discount indefinitely. Something has to give,” the firm said in the letter. Years of underperformance versus peers Land & Buildings also highlighted what it described as sustained underperformance. Over the trailing one-, three- and five-year periods, Invitation Homes has lagged the S&P 500, the broader REIT index, its closest peer American Homes 4 Rent and the proxy peer group the board uses for benchmarking executive compensation, the letter said. Over the past three years, Invitation Homes ranks second to last in that compensation peer group, trailing the group average by more than 35 percentage points, according to Land & Buildings. Shareholders who held the stock for five years have lost more than 20% of their investment, including dividends, the letter said, even as U.S. home prices have continued to climb. The firm noted that Invitation Homes’ shares now trade at an implied capitalization rate of about 7%, roughly 60 basis points wider than American Homes 4 Rent, and at a lower multiple of adjusted funds from operations. The stock trades only modestly above its $20 IPO price from early 2017 while national home prices are up nearly 80% over that period, according to the letter. Capital allocation and legal settlements under scrutiny Land & Buildings blamed Invitation Homes’ strategy for much of the gap. The company was a net buyer of homes in every year from 2022 through 2025 despite “a poor cost of capital,” and earnings have “repeatedly fallen short of expectations,” the firm said. The letter also pointed to legal and regulatory costs. Land & Buildings said Invitation Homes has paid more than $79 million to resolve four legal matters related to resident treatment and business practices, including a $48 million settlement with the Federal Trade Commission in 2024. At the same time, the board approved more than $25 million in special retention awards in March 2026 for the CEO and three other executives, according to the firm. “This troubling misalignment and lack of accountability is deeply concerning,” Land & Buildings said. Call for $2 billion a year in capital returns The activist laid out a three-part plan it says could unlock value and narrow the discount to net asset value: Commit to at least $2 billion a year in capital returns. Land & Buildings wants Invitation Homes to pledge to return a minimum of $2 billion annually to shareholders on a leverage-neutral basis, funded by selling homes individually into the for-sale market. Capital could be returned through share repurchases or special dividends for as long as the stock trades below estimated NAV. Offer renters a path to homeownership. The plan calls for providing existing tenants a 6% rebate to cover a down payment if they buy the home they rent. Land & Buildings argues that rebate roughly matches the brokerage, repair and vacancy costs of an open-market sale, allowing the company to expand homeownership opportunities “for thousands of renters at little or no incremental cost.” Scale back acquisitions and development. The firm recommended Invitation Homes “significantly curtail external growth activities” while its cost of capital is elevated, saying there is “no better use of the Company’s capital than its own stock.” Land & Buildings estimated that a multi-year, programmatic asset sale and capital return program could deliver “substantial annual accretion” to both earnings and NAV per share, supported by what it pegged as nearly $40 billion of gross asset value. Pushback on ‘half measures’ and new director The letter criticized what Land & Buildings characterized as incremental steps by Invitation Homes, including recent home sales and share repurchases, arguing those moves have not been sized or communicated in a way that would change how investors value the company. “Half measures appear to be this Board’s modus operandi: do just enough to relieve pressure while preserving the status quo,” the firm wrote. items.title: Where Developers Are Trying To Lease Public Lands To Build Data Centers
items.description: More than a dozen huge pieces of public land may soon be part of the United States’ arsenal in the global race for artificial intelligence supremacy. The Bureau of Land Management and the Department of Energy are considering leasing at least 17 public land parcels totaling 19,200 acres to developers that plan to build data centers and power infrastructure on the land, a Bisnow analysis of public records found. Just two companies are responsible for more than half of the filings. “This is a new strategy by the Trump administration,” said Chinonso Anozie, an assistant professor at the University of Houston Law Center. “What it would do is remove a lot of local opposition and local vetoes over some of these data centers, limiting what states and local communities can also do in challenging and stopping data centers.” Flickr/Bureau of Land Management The Morley Nelson Snake River Birds of Prey National Conservation Area in Idaho, where the Bureau of Land Management is considering leasing a parcel of public land for a data center development Bisnow verified 17 proposed projects with the BLM and DOE that are either approved or pending authorization by cross-referencing federal agency records and press releases with data center trackers from two conservation and public lands advocacy groups: the Center for Western Priorities and More Than Just Parks . The majority of those projects, excluding separate land parcels for power stations, are in the western U.S., while a smattering of sites are in the Southeast. The filings show that developers are jumping on the opportunity to lease public lands, catalyzed by a July 2025 White House initiative to accelerate the country’s AI industry and by last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act . Using public lands also means the federal government can flex the supremacy clause, a constitutional provision that gives federal law priority over some state laws . This tool could help developers skirt a broad cultural pushback against data centers. Industry advocacy group Data Center Coalition praised the Trump administration and the DOE for the policy initiative. “The digital infrastructure that data centers provide is essential to advancing America’s global economic competitiveness, safeguarding national security, and maintaining the country’s edge in cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and many other 21st-century technologies,” Michele Nellenbach, the trade group’s vice president of federal affairs, said in a statement. But elected officials are already speaking out against leasing public lands for data center development in Idaho and Kentucky. A lack of local support could still hamper proposals far away from towns and cities, said John Boyd Jr., principal at site selection firm The Boyd Co. “Companies routinely look for some type of public-private partnership, whether that be sales tax abatements for the server equipment or property tax abatements,” Boyd said. “All of that requires county, city or state support.” Most of the companies that filed prelease applications with the BLM or have been selected for projects on DOE land didn't respond to Bisnow ’s requests for comment. SB Energy In Ohio Part of a former uranium enrichment plant near the 2,200-person town of Piketon in southern Ohio is planned to become the world’s largest data center to date. SB Energy, a SoftBank Group company, broke ground on the 189-acre project in March and committed to building 10 gigawatts of new power generation connecting to the local grid. It expects to generate 10,000 construction jobs and 2,000 permanent jobs in the region. Known as the Portsmouth Site, it includes Department of Energy land. It is split between public land and some private land, according to a spokesperson for SB Energy. Flickr/U.S. Department of Energy Excavation of the Portsmouth site in 2012 as part of soil remediation efforts at the former uranium enrichment plant Valar Atomics In Utah Valar Atomics, a company focused on scaling nuclear energy for heavy industrial power, filed an application with BLM to build a 9,000-acre facility in Carbon County, Utah, NPR reported in September . BLM records confirm the filing but don't contain the project's acreage. The development, named Project Beehive, is planned to include data centers along with 456 small nuclear reactors and space to produce nuclear fuel and store nuclear waste on a Department of Energy site. A Brookfield Partnership In Kentucky A partnership between Brookfield, NextEra Energy Resources, Big Rivers Electric Corp., Jackson Purchase Energy Cooperative and Paducah Power System is planning an energy generation and AI campus on a 785-acre DOE site. Construction is expected to conclude on the former Superfund site in 2031, following remediation efforts that are needed because of the site’s decades of uranium enrichment operations, according to a release from the department. A spokesperson for the Paducah American Energy Hub told Bisnow in a statement that the team is “committed to working with all stakeholders.” “We have met with many local and state officials and look forward to engaging constructively with them and the community as a whole,” the spokesperson said. Andy Beshear told Politico in August that the Trump administration excluded him from conversations about the $100B data center project and indicated a willingness to block or delay data centers from opening. items.title: Activist investor pressures Invitation Homes to pull back
items.description: An activist investor is pushing for Invitation Homes to change its approach. Jonathan Litt’s Land & Buildings Investment Management is pressuring the single-family rental operator, the Wall Street Journal reported . After failed talks with management and the board, Litt is planning an appeal to company investors in a letter. The hedge fund, which owns less than 1 percent of Invitation as of the second quarter, is calling for Dallas Tanner’s firm to sell properties until the share price catches up with the underlying value of its assets. Shares closed last week at $26.85 each, almost $19 off of Land & Buildings’ estimated value. Litt is calling for the Dallas-based company to return at least $2 billion annually to investors through share repurchases and dividends. It is also seeking for the firm to slow acquisition and development activity and provide a 6 percent down-payment rebate to tenants who ultimately buy their rental homes. Invitation is one of the largest landlords in the single-family rental space, owning almost 86,000 properties as of September. It has a market value of roughly $15.5 billion. The firm’s share price has dwindled by more than 30 percent over the past five years amid rising interest rates. The activist push also seems to be in response to the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, which bars institutional investors, or those that own 350 or more homes, from buying single-family houses (with plenty of exceptions). In a statement, a spokesperson for Invitation Homes said its board of directors and management team are “committed to acting in the best interests of the Company and its shareholders to deliver long-term, sustainable value.” SIGN UP “Members of our Board and management team have had numerous discussions with Land & Buildings over the past several months to better understand its views, as we would with any shareholder,” said the firm. “While we are disappointed that Land & Buildings has chosen to make its issues public at this time, we remain open to further engagement.” Mega landlords such as Invitation, Pretium and Blackstone’s Tricon Residential can still buy rental houses if they make significant renovations or give tenants a chance to buy the properties. Institutions can also buy and sell homes to each other, or purchase properties developed exclusively for renting – a “built-to-rent” model that’s now the industry’s preferred path to growth. But even the threat of the corporate ban on single-family home rentals cast a pall on investment, despite the largest landlords saying they represented a small slice of the number of U.S. homes; firms owning more than 1,000 houses represented 3 percent of the single-family properties available for rent, according to a recent study from the Urban Institute. — Holden Walter-Warner Read more Commercial National Activist investor pushes Six Flags to sell real estate

items.title: Rising rents draw Wall Street money to industrial outdoor storage lot investments across the U.S.
items.description: Hottest outdoor storage property markets The numbers help explain the appetite. Rents for industrial outdoor storage roughly doubled across eight major markets between 2020 and the third quarter of this year, according to data from Newmark Research and Alterra IOS, an owner of such properties. Average rent per usable acre rose 103.5%, to nearly $11,000 a month, compared with a 66% increase for traditional industrial space, such as indoor warehouses. Rent growth, according to Alterra, is most closely tied to infrastructure and energy activity in the area, even more so than data center development specifically. The value of these properties can also increase if located near a seaport, rail line, or highway. But the gains weren't uniform. Baltimore (204%), Houston (159%) and Norfolk (148%) led, while South Florida and Savannah IOS actually trailed traditional industrial. Lisa DeNight, managing director, head of North American industrial research at Newmark, said that Savannah's IOS vacancy remains quite tight despite the rent figures. Recent port activity is a potential factor, according to Alterra. Savannah's container volumes more than doubled between 2010 and 2022 but have since declined, while Houston saw roughly 15% growth from 2022 to 2025. Petrillo said that there is still plenty of room left for values to increase, so an investor jumping in now hasn't missed the game. "We are still in the very early innings," Petrillo said. Sam Cheema co-founder of CanTex Capital, a Dallas-based firm that acquires overlooked industrial real estate in Texas, is seeing increased demand for these lots. "It comes down to supply and demand," he said. "If you need a warehouse you can usually find one. Properly zoned infill IOS sites are much harder to find and every year more of them are converted to warehouses and other uses," he said, referencing multifamily housing units. The scarcity makes tenants sticky. "So a limited supply keeps shrinking. And because so much of the value is in the land itself, owners keep the option to redevelop the site as the area grows," Cheema added. Because of the imbalance of supply and demand, rents and prices are rising across the board, according to Cheema, but no two IOS properties look alike, which has kept the door open for smaller investors. "Big institutions want exposure to IOS, but ownership is fragmented across mom-and-pop owners and small businesses, so it's hard to deploy large amounts of capital without first aggregating these assets into portfolios," Cheema said. Unlike traditional warehouses, there's no standard spec like square footage or clear height to compare them. "That lack of standardization along with the ongoing growth of the asset class, means there's still runway for small investors to find opportunities," Cheema said. "Financing has improved as more lenders have a better understanding of IOS, but it's still largely local and regional banks," Cheema added. Zoning is the biggest challenge. "If you don't understand the city's plans for the area, you may end up owning a use they're trying to phase out," Cheema said. CanTex Capital works with the city and neighborhoods before buying to ensure the impact aligns with the community's plan for its future. Advantages over traditional industrial, multifamily real estate Alex Sutterer, an executive vice president at NAI Hiffman, a Chicago-area commercial real estate firm, said that beyond being a place to store big equipment, IOS attracts investors for two main reasons: lower capital expenditure requirements than traditional industrial or multifamily properties and the potential for higher yields. "Capital improvements are also less specific to individual tenants, so owners can direct spending toward the property's overall functionality," Sutterer said. For private investors, IOS typically trades at a yield around one percentage point higher than traditional industrial properties, helping attract smaller investors and family offices. "We believe that gap will continue to narrow as more institutional capital enters this space," Sutterer added. Even for industrial properties with similar yields, he said the credit profile of tenants is generally stronger for IOS. Shallow-bay, multitenant industrial properties — industrial facilities that tend to be much smaller than big-box distribution warehouses — have comparable yields. Buyer demand remains highly concentrated in the hottest markets, where listings attracted 2.6 times the national average number of views per property. The Midwest and Northeast were the only regions represented in the Top 20 for the 37th consecutive month. The list was evenly split this month, with 10 markets in the Midwest and 10 in the Northeast. Homes in the hottest markets moved significantly faster than the national norm, with median time on market of 37 days, more than 3 weeks faster than the national norm. Among large U.S. metros, Jacksonville, FL posted the biggest year-over-year improvement, jumping 70 spots to rank 189th nationally. Nationwide, the typical payment shock for a repeat homebuyer is $1,100 or an 85% jump over their current $1,300 mortgage payment. But in some of the least locked-in markets, the jump is under 50%. These are typically areas with higher outstanding mortgage rates, and lower home prices. This is quite a contrast from the high-cost coastal markets concentrated in the Northeast and California. In these areas, owners have lower existing rates and a new payment at today’s price and rate is well more than double the typical existing mortgage payment. Today’s housing market is unique in that we’ve seen the amount of equity in the market rise to record-highs . And here the findings are particularly interesting. Even though debt is less widespread among older householders when compared to younger homeowners, the share of debt for this age group has actually increased, meaning that the share who own their homes without a mortgage has decreased compared to 2010! Jiayi notes that this could have implications for the Generational Housing Succession expected over the next decade. items.description: Who Owns Outright? Mortgage Status, Lock-In and Senior Homeownership By Jiayi Xu Nov 16, 2026 Tax Bill Survey Highlights The share of owner-occupied homes owned outright continues to grow. In 2025, 41% of owner-occupied homes were owned free and clear, and 59% still carried a mortgage. Mortgage shares fell across all four regions. The West has the highest share of homes with a mortgage, and the South has the lowest. At the state level, the District of Columbia has the highest share of homes with a mortgage (73.5%), and West Virginia has the lowest (43.4%). Among the 50 largest metros, Washington, DC has the highest share of homes with a mortgage (73.6%), and Miami has the lowest (54.1%). More households aged 75+ own their homes, and more owners carry a mortgage Homeownership among households aged 75+ rose to 78.3% in 2025, up from 75.7% in 2010. The mortgage-free share among owners aged 75+ fell from 79.7% to 71.3%. Most still own outright, but the share with a loan rose from 20.3% to 28.7%. Among the 50 largest metros, mortgages are least common among owners aged 75+ in Grand Rapids, MI, and most common in Riverside, CA. Lock-in from a high-rate environment can shape the timing of the generational housing handoff. Owners with low-rate loans may hold onto their homes longer, while owners who own outright can make decisions on their own schedule. Mortgage rates have been a central constraint on the housing market, and rate changes affect markets differently depending not only on how the mortgage rates that current homeowners pay differ from the market , but also on how much of the housing stock is financed. Areas where owners rely more heavily on mortgages are more sensitive to rate changes, because monthly payments and the cost of moving both rise with borrowing costs. Areas with a higher share of outright ownership are less exposed and may feel smaller effects from rate shocks because residents who own their homes outright are likely indifferent to changes in borrowing costs. With mortgage rates back above 7% and potential Federal Funds rate hikes in 2027 , the lock-in effect is likely to tighten the market again . Owners with low-rate loans are reluctant to give up their rate, which keeps homes off the market. One channel through which these effects accumulate is generational housing succession . The oldest baby boomers, born in 1946, turned 80 in 2026, and as this generation moves into its 80s, a growing number of the homes they own will be released back to the open market. Lock-in from a high-rate environment can shape the timing of that handoff: owners with low-rate loans may hold onto their homes longer, while owners who own outright can make decisions on their own schedule. To understand the differences in geographic impact of high mortgage rates, we use the 2025 1-Year Estimate from the American Community Survey. According to the data, 59% of homeowners in the United States lived in homes with a mortgage and 41% of owners owned their homes free and clear. In fact, the share of homeowners with debt has dropped consistently in recent years, leading to an increase in outright homeownership. In 2010, the share of homes with debt was 67.2% and the share of outright ownership was 32.8%. Figure 1: Increase in the Proportion of Homes Owned Outright Amid a Decrease in Mortgaged Homes In line with national patterns, the share of homes with mortgages declined across all four regions. The West consistently exhibited the highest debt incidence, reflecting greater reliance on financing, with 63.8% of homeowners carrying a mortgage in 2025. By contrast, the South recorded the lowest share at 56.8%. The Northeast and Midwest were tied at 58.7%. In these markets, higher rates are more likely to slow housing activity. By contrast, homeowners in West Virginia (43.4%), Mississippi (47.3%), New Mexico (50.0%), Louisiana (50.9%) and North Dakota (51.1%) are less reliant on home mortages, so housing activity in these states is likely to be affected more mildly. items.description: Report: Demand Surges for Single-Family Rentals Single-family rental demand is rising nationwide, with demand up 24.3% year over year as the cost of homeownership continues to outpace renting. Home Agents November 12, 2026, 3 pm Reading Time: 3 mins read Zillow’s latest Rental Market Report shows that demand for renting single-family homes has risen, with consumers noting that they would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly costs of owning a home, even before saving for a down payment. Nationally, the typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, compared with $2,603 a month to own a single-family home with 20% down, or $360 more each month. “For a growing number of households, renting a house is a legitimate financial strategy,” said Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow. “You get many of the lifestyle benefits, but it takes less income than owning and keeps more flexibility in the monthly budget. That’s the appeal for the deliberate renter.” The size of the raise depends on the market According to Zillow, the pay raise needed to buy is now the highest since early 2025, more than double the $6,463 it took in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly fell below 6%. The gap looks very different from market to market. It’s largest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than double the income needed to rent ($190,561), a gap of $214,364. The next largest gap is in San Francisco ($139,353), followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual gaps are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require a raise. Even with such a raise, would-be buyers still face another hurdle: saving a 20% down payment. About 30% of mortgage buyers use a gift or loan from family or friends, and 46% draw on two or more sources, including the use of down payment assistance programs , according to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report . In addition to the monthly cost, households deciding between renting and buying should weigh the upfront costs of buying, the chance to build equity and the opportunity for renters to invest their down payment instead. Zillow’s rent vs. buy research puts the national break-even timeline—the number of years a household would need to own before buying comes out ahead—at 7.8 years with 20% down. Rental demand keeps climbing As renting a house becomes an increasingly better value, more shoppers are turning to rentals. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for multifamily rentals. Rental demand surges in the Bay Area and the Sun Belt Demand rose the most in San Jose, where ZORDI is up 78.9% from a year ago, followed by San Francisco (60.5%), Austin (59.6%), Miami (51.5%) and Jacksonville (47.9%). San Jose and San Francisco are also among the markets where buying is furthest out of reach, and where rents are rising quickly, up 8.9% and 12.2% respectively. In Austin, Miami and Jacksonville, rent growth is more moderate, at 1.1%, 2.1% and 2.6%. Not every market is following the national trend. ZORDI is down year over year in Providence (-4.3%), Richmond (-1.9%), Baltimore (-1.7%), Hartford (-1.3%) and Washington, D.C. (-0.9%). For more information, visit www.zillow.com . items.description: Single-Family Permitting Weakens While Multifamily Activity Remains Stronger November 16, 2026 Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington No Comments Residential permitting activity continued to show divergent trends across the single-family and multifamily sectors through September 2026. Single-family permitting remained under pressure, with year-to-date activity declining from a year earlier amid ongoing housing affordability challenges and elevated construction costs. In contrast, multifamily permitting recorded growth, reflecting stronger activity in several regions and states. Over the first nine months of the year, the number of single-family permits issued nationwide reached 689,884. Compared with the same period in 2025, this represents a 3.0% decline from the September 2025 total of 711,020. In contrast, multifamily permitting activity remained stronger, with 393,778 permits issued nationwide, marking a 4.1% increase compared with the same period last year. Regionally, year-to-date single-family permitting declined in three out of the four regions through September. The Midwest was the only region to post an increase, with single-family permits rising 0.6%. The South declined 1.9%, the West fell 5.7%, and the Northeast posted the largest decline at 11.8%. Multifamily permits increased in three of the four regions, led by the Northeast (28.2%), followed by the West (9.7%), and the Midwest (5.3%). The South was the only region to post a decline, with multifamily permits falling 5.8%, driven largely by reduced permitting activity in major metropolitan areas across the region. At the state level, 19 states and the District of Columbia recorded increases in single-family permits compared with the same period last year, with gains ranging from 45.5% in the District of Columbia to 0.5% in Wisconsin. The remaining 31 states posted declines. Nevada recorded the steepest decline, with single-family permits falling 25.2%. The ten states issued the highest number of single-family permits accounted for 62.2% of all single-family permits issued nationwide. Texas led the nation with 108,433 permits issued through September 2026, although this represented a 3.1% decline from the same period in 2025. Florida, the second-highest state, recorded a 0.6% decline, while North Carolina, ranking third, posted a 7.9% decrease. Through September, 29 states and the District of Columbia recorded increases in multifamily building permits, while 21 states experienced declines. Kansas posted the largest percentage increase, with multifamily permits rising 99.6%, from 3,041 to 6,071 units. In contrast, Vermont recorded the steepest decline, with permits falling 72.1%, from 982 to 274 units. The ten states issued the highest number of multifamily permits accounted for 60.8% of all multifamily permits issued nationwide. Through the first nine months of 2026, Texas, which issued the largest number of multifamily permits, posted a 17.9% decline compared with the same period last year. California, the second-highest state, recorded a 23.2% increase, while Florida, ranking third, saw multifamily permits decrease by 24.2%. items.description: Realpage Economy Express Episode 75 by Arben Skivjani Posted November 13, 2026 in Insights A surprisingly strong jobs report and stubborn inflation have all but settled the Fed's December decision, even as households and homebuyers keep feeling the squeeze. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the October jobs report showed 165,000 new jobs, almost three times what forecasters expected. Unemployment slipped to 4.1%, and paychecks grew 0.4% in a single month, the fastest pace since January. Job openings climbed to 7.5 million in September, more than expected, even though hiring remains slow. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October and core prices were up 0.3% for the third month in a row, while the annual inflation rate could not be published because prices were never collected during last year's shutdown. Producer prices rose a calmer 0.3% in October after September's jump, but they are still up 6.5% from a year ago, the most since 2022. Fed funds futures pricing now treats a December rate hike as a sure thing, with some traders even betting on a half-point move. The University of Michigan's consumer survey found sentiment rose to 51, the best reading since August, while expected inflation eased to about 4.3%. Federal Reserve data show credit card balances grew in September at their fastest pace in nearly three years. Per the National Association of Realtors, existing home sales fell to their slowest pace since 2010, even with more homes for sale than at any point since 2019. For more information on the state of the U.S. Economy, including forecasts, watch all the episodes of the Economy Express series. items.title: Renter survey: Why fee transparency matters in AI-powered property search
items.description: Renter survey: Why fee transparency matters in AI-powered property search Published Nov. 16, 2026 By Hallie Busta Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print Permission granted by Zillow Sponsored content By Zillow Rentals SPONSORED CONTENT BY Fee transparency is quickly shifting from “nice to have” to a core differentiator for multifamily operators looking to stand out in a crowded market. New data from Zillow, based on a survey of more than 53,700 renters nationwide, found that nearly all (96%) want all fees disclosed, and more than three-quarters (78%) prefer they be bundled into their rent for a single, clear, all-in cost. Prospects wanting to know exactly how much it will cost to live at a property isn’t new, but the arrival of artificial intelligence (AI) in their searches is raising the stakes for operators to answer that question. Zillow found that 28% of recent renters who used AI anywhere in their search used it to negotiate — with this number rising to 37% among those renting in buildings with 50 or more units. AI search lets renters ask specific, plain language questions about a property, and its answers prioritize complete, accurate listings that include all the information renters want to know. “Growing cost concerns and rising AI use should be a catalyst for treating fee transparency as part of the decision experience, not just a disclosure requirement,” says Brian Miller, Principal for Industry & Partnership at Zillow Rentals. Renters’ priorities are shifting The data makes it clear: Today’s renter wants affordability and value. That means amenities and new finishes aren’t as attractive as they once were. Operators that can show how their property delivers on affordability and value (with or without the wellness rooms and bowling alleys ) are more likely to convert prospects into renters and keep them. Rising renter costs are fueling this shift: Security deposits are up roughly $200 year over year, and the share of renters paying at least 1 recurring fee other than for pets rose 11 points during that time, according to the survey data. Meanwhile, the data indicate renters are factoring in their commute and walkability more than before — unsurprising, as fuel prices remain high and volatile across the country. AI is elevating renters’ fee transparency demands AI is changing property search by letting prospects ask highly specific questions to help them decide whether your property meets their needs before they even step foot on-site. Operators should be mindful of this trend: a significant majority (78%) of recent renters used AI at least once during the searching, shopping, or renting process . Top uses for AI during property search, according to Zillow’s survey of recent renters: Home recommendations: 56% Personalized answers about their lease: 45% (for renters at 50+ unit properties, that jumps to 53%) Market insights: 44% Help deciding whether to rent or buy: 37% Negotiating on their behalf: 28% (37% for renters at 50+ unit properties) Zillow AI mode data shows today’s prospective renters are asking about cost early in the process. “Pricing and fees” is the third-most-common search topic in AI mode, following location and amenities. Renters want to know more than the advertised “monthly rent.” They expect to see information about fees, utilities, required deposits, parking, internet access, and other recurring expenses. Clear, consistent cost information across listings is essential for operators that want to stay competitive in the new world of AI-enabled property search. Property comparisons account for 40% of recent renter prompts in Zillow’s AI mode. That’s evidence renters are turning to AI to answer a question listings too often leave unresolved: Which home is right for me, and what will it actually cost to live there? What this means for operators AI is a new path to discovery and consideration. The more detailed the listing, especially in how it anticipates prospects’ affordability concerns, the more likely it is to be found by AI and influence renters’ decisions. To ensure property listings include the affordability information that renters want and that AI tools will look for, operators should: Show the full required monthly cost upfront. Clearly separate mandatory charges from optional add-ons and one-time fees. Keep cost information consistent wherever a property is listed. “Renters cite evaluating and comparing properties as their biggest pain point nearly twice as often as they do finding listings,” Miller says. “Hidden fees, inconsistent pricing, and missing amenity details make it harder to compare, undermining trust and making it harder for renters to confidently choose their property.” Get the full picture of today’s renter AI lets prospects compare already available information about a property. But it can’t fill the information gaps operators leave. By publishing clear, detailed, and consistent information about all costs associated with a property on every platform it’s advertised, operators can ensure their properties show up where renters are looking — and with the right information to answer questions and move renters forward in their consideration. items.description: HAR named among defendants in new Compass litigation by Emily Marek November 16, 2026 HAR is one of 15 MLSs named in a new slate of Compass lawsuits. Compass filed new antitrust lawsuits against 15 different MLSs, with the Houston Association of REALTORS ’® Houston Realtors Information Service, Inc., named among the defendants. All MLSs named in Compass’ new slate of suits have rules that require real estate agents to share listings with the MLS when they begin publicly marketing those properties, a practice that directly contradicts Compass’ highly contested three-phase marketing strategy . “Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass representative said in a press release. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.” In its complaint against HAR, Compass called the association a “competition-killing real estate industry organization” and asserted that HRIS and its “co-conspirators” have banded together to “deprive homeowners of choice.” In addition to HAR, the listing services named in Compass lawsuits include: Arizona Regional MLS bridgeMLS Bay East MLS Canopy MLS Contra Costa MLS Doorify MLS Hive MLS MLSListings The MLS-CLAW NorthstarMLS OneKey MLS REcolorado San Diego MLS Stellar MLS Compass maintains that the lawsuits will ultimately decide whether homeowners or MLSs get to decide how properties are marketed. “It’s almost as if these MLSs are asking people to ignore the evidence that proves their claims aren’t true,” the Compass representative added. “For years, seven of the top 25 MLSs, covering 340,000 agents across 12 states, have allowed agents to publicly market ‘office exclusives’ without fines, and none of the problems they warn about have happened. If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30% of the country?” HAR declined to comment. items.title: Agencies extend comment period for proposed third-party risk management guidance
items.description: Agencies extend comment period for proposed third-party risk management guidance Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Office of the Comptroller of the Currency National Credit Union Administration For release at 4:15 p.m. EST Share --> --> --> --> --> --> The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Federal Reserve Board, the National Credit Union Administration, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that they will extend, until December 16, the comment period for proposed guidance on managing risks associated with third-party relationships. Comments on the proposal were originally due November 16. The proposed guidance reflects the agencies' supervisory experience and lessons learned from examining financial institutions' third-party risk management practices. It is intended to help banks and credit unions tailor their risk management practices to the risks associated with individual third-party relationships. The proposed guidance takes a principles-based approach and, like all supervisory guidance, is non-binding. When finalized, the federal bank regulatory agencies plan to rescind existing third-party risk management guidance and replace it with the finalized guidance to promote consistency and prudent innovation in the banking industry. NCUA also plans to rescind its existing third-party risk management guidance and will conduct its own reviews to update related guidance as needed. Also today, the Federal Reserve Board separately announced that it will extend, until December 16, the comment period on a proposed third-party risk management guide specifically for Federal Reserve-supervised traditional community banks. items.title: Phoenix’s housing correction isn’t over, but Scottsdale tells a different story
items.description: Phoenix’s housing correction isn’t over, but Scottsdale tells a different story by Phoenix Agent November 13, 2026 Anne Hartnett Hi, I'm Anne Hartnett and I am here with real estate economist Matthew Gardner to chat about our Q3 update. How are you, Matthew? Matthew Gardner I am well, Anne, how are you? Hartnett I'm great, thanks. So we've been waiting years for housing transactions to recover. At what point do we stop calling this a cyclical showdown and recognize that something more fundamental has changed in how Americans buy and sell homes? Gardner Great question. I mean, the short answer, as far as I'm concerned, is that we should have stopped calling it a cycle, or cyclical, about a year ago, because the forces that are holding sales down now aren't really the kind that are cycle-fixes. So let me explain. When existing home sales, we know, fell from over 6 million a year in 2021 to about 4 million in 2023, and they've been stuck there for nearly three years now. September numbers came in at 3.99 million. Now, there are three structural forces that explain this: One, the mortgage rate itself has become an asset that people just won't sell. I mean, in the second quarter, 49% of outstanding mortgages carried a rate at below 4%. Now, a record 43% were originated between mid-2019 and mid-2022. That means that selling gives up that loan — and that's not a cycle. It's a balance sheet decision, and it decays very slowly. There are some who suggest that the share of mortgages at 6% or higher, which is around 22.5% in Q2, only hits 27% to 29% by mid-2027. That's a slow grind. Now secondly, the buyer pool has aged. Last year, a typical first-time buyer was 40 years old, and a typical repeat buyer was 62. And last year, first-time buyers were 21% of purchases. That's a record low, and roughly half of their pre-2008 share. And a market that runs on equity rather than income, well, it transacts less often. And finally, the ten year Treasury, it's running around 5% today, and the 3% mortgage was a product of a zero-rate world that no reasonable forecast brings back. But this year, it gave us a small test of my belief. Briefly, back in February, mortgage rates dropped to below 6%, just. I think it was at the end of February. Lowest rate since 2022. But by June, they were back up to 6.5. Now they're above 7.3. Now, at that point, when they were very low, NAR had forecast a 14% jump in sales. But what are we doing today? We're running below last year. So the dip was far too brief to prove anything by itself. But in a normal cycle, cheaper money brings buyers back fast. This time it didn't. So the bottom line for me is that 6 million sales a year is the wrong benchmark. 2021 was an anomaly — a once-in-50-year financing, or refinancing, window. In 2019, we sold about 5.3 million existing homes. And my view is that the realistic norm, at least for the rest of this decade? Somewhere between 4 and 4.5 million. And we'll get there through life events such as job changes, divorce, death, downsizing, not through a rate rally. So for brokers, that changes their business model. In a 4 million-unit market, well, the pipeline isn't buyers waiting for rates to fall. It's people who have to move regardless of rate — relocations, estate sales, divorces, retirees. Now those transactions happen at 7%. If your marketing is built around a quote, wait for rates to drop, unquote, well, you're building for a market, unfortunately, that may not show up. Hartnett Housing drives everything from construction and lending to consumer spending. Could several years of depressed transaction volume begin to weigh on broader economic growth? Gardner It already has, but interestingly, not in the way that most people assume. So let's start with what counts. The sale of an existing home is just a transfer of an asset. It doesn't add to GDP or growth. What counts is construction, remodeling and also the services around a transaction — that would be brokerage commissions, and also households buying new furniture, new appliances, that follow any move. Residential investment is only 3.7% of GDP against a historic average of about five. Now, housing’s total share of the economy? About 16%. That's actually still the lowest we've seen since 2019. Now, residential investment shrank for five straight quarters, falling at an annual rate of about 7.8% in Q1. It did tick up a bit in the second quarter. So no doubt housing has been a drag. But the contrarian part is that the economy grew right through it. Nonresidential investment rose 8.5% in the second quarter, driven by AI equipment and also software. Consumer spending rose 3.4%. You see, homeowners are sitting on substantial equity, and that wealth supports spending even when they don't move. Low transactional volumes is a slow leak, not a recession trigger. Now the real risk, as I see it, is actually different. Housing's historically been the economy's shock absorber. A recession hits the Fed cuts rates to stimulate the economy, ultimately mortgage rates drop, housing turns and construction hiring leads to a recovery. Now that channel’s impaired. Ten-year treasury near five, inflation at 3.4, and in early October, markets are still weighing whether the Fed's next move could be to hike in order to address inflation. But if the labor market weakens further — now remember, September we added just 29000 jobs — well, the Fed should be cutting rates, but I just don't see that happening. So we may not get the usual housing-led rebound on the other side. Now where you feel the drag first is local and also sectoral. It's not in GDP. It shows up in title, escrow, mortgage originations, moving companies, furniture retailers and obviously broker incomes, but also shows up in city and state budgets. Supply growth has slowed sharply. Projects totaling nearly 4,400 units have been delivered year to date, down 54% from the same period last year.Area vacancy declined 40 basis points for the second consecutive quarter, reaching 7.4%. Year over year, the rate is down 30 basis points.Apartment rents edged down 0.4% during the past three months to $1,585 per month. Still, rents are up 0.9% from one year ago, supported by steady gains during the first half of 2026.Although sales activity remains below traditional levels, a strong third quarter pushed year-to-date sales well ahead of last year’s pace. Activity through the third quarter is up more than 35% from the same period in 2025. Year to date, the median sale price is $218,000 per unit, up 8% from 2025.Raleigh-Durham multifamily market overviewVacancy in the Raleigh-Durham multifamily market continued to improve as supply growth tapered off, with the rate falling 80 basis points during the past six months. Year to date, renter demand remains well above traditional levels but trails the pace recorded in the same periods of 2024 and 2025. Demand has been concentrated in Central Raleigh and North Cary/Morrisville, which together accounted for nearly 30% of the market’s net move-ins totaling more than 8,500 units during the past year. Central Raleigh illustrates the sharp slowdown in supply growth across the broader market. From 2023 to 2025, more than 5,200 units were delivered in the submarket, compared with just 250 units year to date. Additionally, fewer than 400 units are currently under construction in Central Raleigh, down from a pipeline peak of roughly 4,000 units in late 2022.Total sales in the Raleigh-Durham multifamily investment market picked up in recent months after a slow first half. Sales during the third quarter nearly matched the total recorded in the preceding six months. Activity has been concentrated in a handful of submarkets year to date, with Central Raleigh, Northwest Raleigh, North Cary/Morrisville, and Northeast Raleigh accounting for 75% of transactions through the third quarter. As discussed in our June 24 article, “Title X of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act: What Real Estate Developers, Investors and Lenders Need to Know” (the “ Initial Article ”), Title X of the Act generally bars a “ large institutional investor ” from buying—or entering into a contract to buy—a “ single-family home ” unless a statutory exception applies. Under the Act, a covered investor must be a qualifying for-profit entity engaged in the single-family rental (“ SFR ”) business that, alone or with others acting “ in concert ,” has direct or indirect “ investment control ” over at least 350 single-family homes. Homes acquired through statutory exceptions after July 11, 2026, are excluded from that count. For this purpose, a “ single-family home ” generally means a structure with no more than two dwelling units, excluding manufactured homes. On October 23, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury (the “ Treasury ”) issued proposed regulations under Title X (proposed 31 C.F.R. Part 36, the “ Proposed Regulations ”). The Proposed Regulations explain several exceptions for build-to-rent (“ BTR ”), renovate-to-rent, homeownership programs, creditor enforcement and institutional resales, as well as rules affecting investment funds and managers. However, some of the Treasury’s proposals could also complicate common BTR development and sale structures. As of the date hereof, the Proposed Regulations are not binding or final, and the Treasury expects additional rulemakings. Public comments on the Proposed Regulations will be due by November 23, 2026, and the statutory purchase prohibition under the Act becomes effective January 7, 2027, independent of when final regulations are adopted. Key Takeaways The headline for BTR is mixed: the Treasury proposes a purchase deadline of 18 months after a home receives its certificate of occupancy, but also confirms that qualifying homes can be resold repeatedly between covered institutional investors. The Treasury also proposes a written-program requirement for several exceptions and a more detailed test for passive investors. Important gaps remain that are unresolved in the Proposed Regulations, including how the Act applies to fund aggregation, equity transfers, pre-effective-date purchase contracts and BTR homes leased before an institutional sale. The discussion below distinguishes what Congress expressly provided in the Act from the additional conditions the Treasury now offers in the in the Proposed Regulations. BTR Protection: Greater Certainty, but a Narrower Initial Acquisition Window The Act expressly allows purchases under a BTR program in which a large institutional investor “ purchases, constructs, or constructs and retains ” newly constructed homes to be managed as rentals. Our Initial Article explained why that language appeared to protect traditional BTR development and institutional takeout sales. The Treasury’s proposed definition, however, focuses on when a home is purchased and how it is first occupied. Proposed § 36.5 would require a home acquired under the BTR exception to (i) have no previous owner-occupant, (ii) be purchased within 18 months after its certificate of occupancy (or local equivalent), and (iii) be first occupied by renters after the purchase. The Treasury rejected an alternative that would treat an older home as “ newly constructed ” solely because it was originally built and continuously used as a rental. The proposal does not separately explain how these purchase-focused requirements apply when an institutional investor itself constructs and retains the homes, a scenario the Act expressly includes. This may matter for merchant-builders that deliver a community in phases, lease homes as they are completed and sell the stabilized project in one transaction. Because the proposed deadline is tied to each home’s certificate of occupancy, earlier phases could fall outside the proposed BTR exception even while later phases qualify. The Treasury has not proposed a project-wide extension measured from the final phase or stabilization. Another statutory exception may be needed for homes that miss the 18-month window. A second issue concerns lease-up before closing. The proposed § 36.5(c) states that homes must be “ after the purchase, first occupied by renters .” That language appears to require that first-time rental occupancy occur after the institutional buyer purchases the homes, so a home already renter-occupied before sale would appear ineligible for this exception. The Proposed Regulations do not expressly disqualify pre-leased homes or analyze pre-sale lease-up, so clarification remains warranted before buyers rely on this exception. The Act permits BTR homes in both entirely rental and mixed rental/owner-occupied communities, and the Treasury confirms that the exception is not lost simply because a development also contains other property types. The rule still applies home-by-home: conventional apartment buildings with three or more dwelling units per structure generally fall outside the Act’s definition of “ single-family home ,” while qualifying SFR homes within the same development remain subject to the applicable exception. items.title: The seasonal decline in housing inventory is in full force
items.description: Housing inventory Housing inventory has picked up recently, after mortgage rates went above 6.64% and then shot up toward 7.60%. Inventory growth had been very tame this year, with some weeks negative year over year. As housing inventory returns to normal levels, it takes weaker demand to get stronger growth and rates moving toward 7.60% did that. Still, it's more about sales taking longer to happen and demand being hit, because new listings data didn’t budge much recently. Now, we are in the full-blown seasonal decline as we get ready to prep for spring 2027. Inventory growth is running at 7.11% over last year even with easier comps, as last year demand was running toward a 9-month high in December of 2025. Weekly inventory change (Nov. 6-Nov. 13): Inventory fell from 902,740 to 895,988 Same week last year (Nov. 7-Nov. 14): Inventory fell from 842,257 to 836,487 New listings New listings have been in their seasonal decline since June and nothing abnormal with this data line has happened in 2026; in fact, it’s been the best year of new listings since 2022. One concern I had about higher rates is that more people might simply not list their homes — as they did in the second half of 2022 due to higher rates. However, that hasn’t happened; we did see a more noticeable year-over-year decline this last week, but for the most part it’s been a healthy year. In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years . Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years: 2026: 53,162 2025: 56,569 Price-cut percentage Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%. At that point demand fell and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%. In my 2026 home-price forecast, I called for a national decline of -0.62% for the year. Home-price growth really isn’t going anywhere this year and my -0.62% forecast may be hard to achieve, since most home-price indices show growth between 1% and 2%. However, with higher rates and a rising price-cut percentage, we will be closer to the forecast. Clearly, if rates hadn’t risen above 6.75%, pricing data wouldn’t have shown the recent slowdown. The price-cut percentage for last week: 2026: 43.% 2025: 42% 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% Last week wasn’t good for mortgage rates or the bond market: we had hawkish Fed statements and hot inflation data. We were getting closer to mortgage rates below 7% for the holidays, but they made a big reversal from 7.17% to 7.50%. In addition, President Trump talked about raising tariffs against Mexico and we still have no deal with Iran. Pretty much everything you needed for rates to go lower went the other way — something I talked about in this episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief Sarah Wheeler. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they did improve last week. Traditionally, when mortgage rates escalate with the 10-year yield and then make a big reversal — like we just had from a 5.35% 10-year yield top that dropped down toward 4.82% — spreads do get worse to try to compress mortgage rate volatility. However, we had a big reversal higher, and spreads improved some as the 10-year yield rose toward 5.14%. Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads fell to 2.13% from 2.27% a week earlier. Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle. If we had the best levels of spreads in 2026, mortgage rates would be 7.19% today, not 7.50% . If we had the worst mortgage spread levels of 2023, mortgage rates would be 8.48% today, not 7.17% . Weekly pending sales Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data. The key for the last four weeks: housing demand has stabilized, as our weekly pending sales have shown. Now, higher rates most likely will impact this week’s data more than last week, but the last four weeks have shown if we can get rates back below 7% and just have them stick, we can work with this. Housing demand typically grows when rates get below 6.64% and fades when rates are above 7%, especially if the move in rates is fast, like we saw recently. Still, it was encouraging to see stabilization in the data when rates were trying to get below 7% again. Of course, we are seeing big year-over-year declines in this data line as rates were heading toward 6% last year. Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years: 2026: 50,623 2025: 60,722 Purchase applications Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. We did have 8% week-to-week growth last week as rates tried to get below 7% the week before. I expect the next purchase application data to get hit as rates picked up. This data was very positive year over year when rates were under 6.64%, but not so much when it headed toward 7% and got to 7.60%. items.description: The coming week holds a packed slate of insights from Realtor.com Economics, as well as vital indicators about the state of the housing market. On Monday, senior economist Jiayi Xu published a report on free and clear mortgages , which breaks down trends in where the most homeowners own their home outright . On Tuesday, senior economist Joel Berner has our third-quarter New-Construction Insights report looking at how new-home prices and homebuilder incentives have trended in the past quarter. Then on Wednesday, Jiayi is back with a look at October rent trends in our monthly rental report, which will also dive deep into how apartment supply shifts are likely to affect the market. Finally, on Thursday, senior economist Anthony Smith will analyze our weekly housing data for clues on the latest trends. Turning to the macro indicators that will be released, both pending home sales and new construction will be released on Wednesday and on Thursday, we’ll see mortgage rates. October pending home sales, released by the National Association of Realtors®, are likely to be low. In September, the pending data hit a series record low , tumbling more than 7% in the month and 11% from a year ago. Realtor.com data showed double-digit declines in both pending sales and new contract signings in October. I think we’re likely to see another tough few months for housing activity as we wrap up 2026. Loading... Similar challenges are likely for builders and the high-rate environment is likely to slow October construction. In September’s construction report from the U.S. Census Bureau, permits, starts, and completions all fell from both the prior month and prior year. Declines were mildest for permits, and single-family fared better than multifamily in starts and completions. Meanwhile, mortgage rates notched a fourth consecutive week of decline last week, getting all the way down to 7.11%, but I think that streak ends this week. Home shoppers planning to take out a mortgage will want to prepare, while home shoppers planning to use cash are likely to find a less-competitive housing market to navigate. Danielle Hale is the chief economist of Realtor.com.

items.title: Apartment rents diverge: San Francisco rises, the Sun Belt falls
items.description: America's apartment landscape has become a tale of two opposing rent trends. Rents are climbing in the Bay Area and the Midwest, while much of the Sun Belt is still sliding. National same-store asking rents edged up 1.7% from a year earlier in October, the biggest annual gain since May 2023, apartment industry data firm RealPage reported Nov. 11. The national figure hides a wide gap. San Francisco rents jumped 14.7%, evidence of why city officials are pressing the supply button to drive housing construction. San Antonio rents dropped 2.6%. The month-over-month picture illustrates less dramatic change. RealPage showed that rents fell 0.7% in October, the first monthly cut of 2026. The company said the annual gain came less from strong pricing than from weak months dropping out of the calculation, making for stronger year-over-year comparables. Other trackers show the same upward drift, with different monthly readings. Yardi Matrix reported rents up 0.1% in October, with annual growth of 1.4%, the strongest in more than three years. Apartments.com put annual growth at 1.6%, even as rents slipped 0.15% for the month. Supply wave cools Supply and demand are edging toward balance. RealPage said renters absorbed nearly 304,800 conventional apartments in the year ending in Q3 2026. Developers completed nearly 318,000 units over the same period, almost half the late-2024 peak. Occupancy eased to 95%, down 20 basis points from September. It is still up 40 basis points this year and 10 basis points above October 2025. Landlords hit the brakes Improving rents haven't translated into a property buying spree. Camden Property Trust , a large apartment landlord, walked away from two acquisitions and canceled two planned development projects. The Federal Reserve's rate hike was a main reason, rental economist Jay Parsons wrote on LinkedIn. Two deals under contract fell through after the hike, Camden CEO Alex Jessett said on the third-quarter earnings call. Camden asked for lower prices, and the sellers declined. Buying also beat building on cost. Camden bought an asset at about $370,000 a door, while building it would have cost north of $600,000, Jessett said. Camden's earnings show an unevenly improving market. Funds from operations, a standard earnings measure for real estate investment trusts, were $1.70 per diluted share in the third quarter. Core funds from operations were $1.71, $0.02 above the company's guidance midpoint. "A higher-for-longer rate environment may equate to a lower-for-longer supply environment," Parsons wrote. Fewer projects penciling out means fewer new apartment options for renters. Coasts and Midwest lead Northern California took the top three spots for rent power among the 50 largest markets, RealPage said. San Francisco rose 14.7%, San Jose 9.5% and Oakland 8.5%. All three are running near 97% occupancy. Midwest metros fill much of the rest of the top 10. Milwaukee led at 4.2%, followed by Chicago at 3.3%, and Kansas City and Cleveland at 3.1% each. Detroit and St. Louis each gained 2.7% and just missed the cut. Sun Belt still lags Most Sun Belt and Florida markets continued to decline. The South as a region returned to annual growth, but only by 0.5%. San Antonio had the deepest decline in rents among big markets at 2.6%. Its occupancy of 92.5% was the lowest of the 50 largest markets. Houston fell 1.8%, followed by drops in Tampa of 1%, Charlotte of 0.9% and Denver of 0.8%. Several Sun Belt markets have turned the corner, however. Jacksonville rose 2.6%, Raleigh 1.0%, Atlanta 0.8%, Austin and Miami 0.6% each, and Phoenix 0.4%. items.description: Renewals Carry Apartment REIT Pricing as Coastal and Sun Belt Results Split by Meggan Taylor Posted November 12, 2026 in REIT Renewals and low turnover continued to support apartment REIT pricing in 3rd quarter 2026, while new lease performance remained pressured across much of the Sun Belt. Results from Camden Property Trust, Essex Property Trust, Mid-America Apartment Communities (MAA), UDR and Vivmark Residential highlighted a sharp divide between coastal and Sun Belt markets, as coastal-heavy operators raised guidance and Sun Belt-focused peers lowered expectations. A merger and major portfolio shifts reshaped the group Vivmark Residential reported its first quarterly results since AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential completed their merger on Aug. 17, creating a same-store portfolio of 157,377 apartment homes. The company raised its target for yearly cost savings and revenue gains from the combination by $10 million to $135 million. COO Michael Manelis said years of separate operations gave Vivmark “a multi-year A/B test,” letting it compare the two companies’ practices and keep what works best. Other operators also changed their portfolio exposure. Camden completed the roughly $1.6 billion sale of 11 California communities on July 29, and UDR formed a $2 billion partnership with Apollo, covering 19 communities. As a result, three of the five REITs now operate meaningfully different portfolios than a year ago. Renewals continued to carry lease pricing Renewals remained the primary source of pricing strength. Renewal lease rates rose 5.3% at Essex, MAA and Vivmark and 3.6% at Camden, while retention remained elevated across portfolios. UDR reported a record-high 3rd quarter retention rate of 52%, and MAA recorded a record-low share (10.1%) of move-outs to homeownership. Management tied that stability largely to housing costs. “We see sustained high homeownership costs, and we see residents continuing to stay in place, both for cyclical and structural reasons,” UDR CFO Dave Bragg said. MAA added that the dollar gap between new and renewal rents has held at about $190 to $200 for four quarters, a small difference next to the cost and hassle of moving. New lease pricing stayed negative as concessions persisted New lease pricing told a different story. New lease rates declined at four of the five REITs, ranging from -6.0% at MAA to -0.2% at Essex. Vivmark was the only exception, with new lease rates up 0.4%. Camden and MAA attributed the weakness largely to lease-up discounting and lease mix. “Concessions have remained remarkably sticky, seemingly led by many merchant builders now turned reluctant operators,” Camden CEO Alex Jessett said. MAA said its year-to-date new lease decline narrows to -1.9% when the departing resident stayed only one lease term, a figure it views as a better gauge of market rents. Northern California and Denver marked the extremes Regional performance diverged sharply. Northern California led results at both Vivmark and Essex, where same-store NOI rose 11.2% and 7.0%, respectively. At UDR, new lease rates rose 5.7% in the West region but fell 7.2% in the Southwest region. Denver sat at the other end, with same-store NOI down 9.6% at Vivmark and nearly 7% at both Camden and MAA. Essex linked Northern California’s strength to limited supply and rents that remain below historical norms relative to incomes. By its estimate, rents could rise more than 20%, assuming no wage growth, before rent-to-income ratios returned to pre-COVID levels. Meanwhile, Camden tied most of its Denver revenue decline to local legislation that stopped it from billing residents for common-area utilities, on top of persistent concessions. Guidance split along portfolio lines Full-year outlooks followed the same divide. Essex, UDR and Vivmark raised same-store revenue guidance, while Camden and MAA lowered theirs. Both Sun Belt-focused REITs cited timing: MAA said new lease pricing is recovering later than expected, and Camden said September was softer than expected. Both still pointed to early improvement as supply eases. “October new resident lease pricing improved from September, counter to the normal seasonal pattern,” MAA CEO Brad Hill said. What to watch in 4th quarter The key question for 4th quarter is whether easing supply translates into firmer revenue growth in Sun Belt markets. With completions declining and demand holding up, those results should show whether supply-heavy markets are beginning to close the gap with coastal markets.
